name: Nok culture
title: The story of the Nok culture

text: About 3,500 years ago, farmers settled in central Nigeria, in West Africa.
They lived in small hamlets, tiny villages of a few homes, and never built towns.
src: c. 1500 BCE: Farming communities settle in central Nigeria / the early ironworkers of West Africa
Excavations have found hamlets and single compounds about the size of a farmstead today / small hamlets without towns

text: They grew pearl millet and ground the grain into flour, probably to cook as porridge.
They also gathered honey and cooked meat in their pots.
src: they grew pearl millet / Grinding stones show that grain was ground into flour, probably to be cooked as porridge
the Nok people were gathering honey about 3,500 years ago and used their pots for meat as well

text: More than 2,900 years ago, they began making hollow clay figures of men and women with large heads.
The figures have holes in their eyes, detailed hairstyles and lots of beaded jewellery.
src: On this view the sculptures first appear about 900 BCE / hollow terracotta figures of great skill / they show men and women standing or seated / The heads are large in proportion to the bodies
the eyes, usually triangular or semicircular beneath arching brows, have pierced pupils / Hairstyles are modelled in great detail / many figures wear necklaces, bracelets and anklets of beads

text: The Nok people were also among the early ironworkers of West Africa, and built furnaces to make iron.
They went on using grinding stones and stone tools beside the new metal.
src: The Nok people were also among the early ironworkers of West Africa / uncovered the bases and walls of smelting furnaces still in place
Grinding stones and other stone tools remained in use alongside the new metal

text: About 2,000 years ago the clay figures stop, and nobody knows why the culture ended.
Thieves have dug up many Nok sites to sell the figures, but archaeologists still study places like Taruga.
src: around the turn of the Common Era the terracottas cease and the culture disappears from the archaeological record. Why it ended is not known

most of the known sites in the Frankfurt project’s research area have been looted / Since 2005 a long-term project of Goethe University Frankfurt ... has surveyed and excavated many sites / Taruga and Samun Dukiya, two sites where sculptures lay undisturbed
